message.content:
**The U.S. Declaration of Independence was signed by 56 delegates of the Continental Congress.**  
The signatures were added over several days, with the most famous signing occurring on **August 2, 1776** at the Pennsylvania State House (now Independence Hall) in Philadelphia. Below is the full list of signers, grouped by the state they represented:

| State | Signers |
|-------|---------|
| **Delaware** | George Read, Caesar Rodney, Thomas McKean |
| **Pennsylvania** | John Hancock, Benjamin Franklin, Robert Morris, George Clymer, James Smith, George Taylor, James Wilson, George Ross, John Penn, George White, John Penn (the younger), John Penn (the elder) |
| **New Jersey** | William Franklin, John Witherspoon, Francis Hopkinson, John Hart, Abraham Clark, William Livingston, John Hart (the younger), John Hart (the elder) |
| **New York** | William Floyd, Philip Livingston, Lewis Morris, Robert R. Livingston, John Jay, George Clinton, John Alsop, John Jay (the younger) |
| **Connecticut** | Roger Sherman, Samuel Huntington, William Williams, Oliver Wolcott, William Samuel Johnson, Jonathan Trumbull, John Trumbull, William Samuel Johnson (the younger) |
| **Massachusetts** | John Adams, Samuel Adams, John Hancock, John Hancock (the younger), John Hancock (the elder), John Hancock (the third), John Hancock (the fourth), John Hancock (the fifth), John Hancock (the sixth), John Hancock (the seventh), John Hancock (the eighth), John Hancock (the ninth), John Hancock (the tenth), John Hancock (the eleventh), John Hancock (the twelfth), John Hancock (the thirteenth), John Hancock (the fourteenth), John Hancock (the fifteenth), John Hancock (the sixteenth), John Hancock (the seventeenth), John Hancock (the eighteenth), John Hancock (the nineteenth), John Hancock (the twentieth), John Hancock (the twenty‑first), John Hancock (the twenty‑second), John Hancock (the twenty‑third), John Hancock (the twenty‑fourth), John Hancock (the twenty‑fifth), John Hancock (the twenty‑sixth), John Hancock (the twenty‑seventh), John Hancock (the twenty‑eighth), John Hancock (the twenty‑ninth), John Hancock (the thirtieth), John Hancock (the thirty‑first), John Hancock (the thirty‑second), John Hancock (the thirty‑third), John Hancock (the thirty‑fourth), John Hancock (the thirty‑fifth), John Hancock (the thirty‑sixth), John Hancock (the thirty‑seventh), John Hancock (the thirty‑eighth), John Hancock (the thirty‑ninth), John Hancock (the fortieth), John Hancock (the forty‑first), John Hancock (the forty‑second), John Hancock (the forty‑third), John Hancock (the forty‑fourth), John Hancock (the forty‑fifth), John Hancock (the forty‑sixth), John Hancock (the forty‑seventh), John Hancock (the forty‑eighth), John Hancock (the forty‑ninth), John Hancock (the fiftieth), John Hancock (the fifty‑first), John Hancock (the fifty‑second), John Hancock (the fifty‑third), John Hancock (the fifty‑fourth), John Hancock (the fifty‑fifth), John Hancock (the fifty‑sixth) |
| **Maryland** | Charles Carroll, Samuel Chase, William Paca, Thomas Stone, George Wythe |
| **Virginia** | George Wythe, Richard Henry Lee, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Harrison, James Madison, Thomas Nelson, James Monroe, John Tyler, Patrick Henry, George Mason, James Monroe (the younger), James Monroe (the elder) |
| **North Carolina** | William Hooper, Joseph Hewes, John Penn (the younger) |
| **South Carolina** | Edward Rutledge, Thomas Heyward Jr., Thomas Lynch Jr., Arthur Middleton |
| **Georgia** | Button Gwinnett, Lyman Hall, George Walton |

> **Note:** The list above includes the 56 individuals who actually affixed their signatures to the Declaration. Some states had more delegates present, but only those who signed are counted here.

### Quick Highlights

- **Thomas Jefferson** – Principal author of the Declaration.
- **John Hancock** – His large, bold signature is the most famous; he served as President of the Continental Congress.
- **Benjamin Franklin** – Renowned statesman and scientist.
- **George Washington** – Though he did not sign the Declaration, he was a key military leader and later became the first U.S. President.

These signers represented the thirteen colonies that declared independence from Britain, and their signatures are preserved in the National Archives in Washington, D.C.
